papers.why: Early warning models miss life events; human outreach must check the story behind every flag.

papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Interviews with 27 online students whose at-risk predictions were wrong. Errors came from unforeseen life events: family and work changes, health, computer problems. Some new data sources could reduce errors.

papers.why: Frames why assessment redesign is part of AI adoption, not just cheating prevention.

papers.finding: Position paper: traditional assessment is hard to design, gives snapshots, is not adapted to learners, fits school culture more than real-world culture, and tests skills humans now do with computers. Reviews AI approaches that partly address this and their new challenges.

children.name: The Early Warning System
children.blurb: An early warning system tracks indicators such as attendance, behavior incidents, and course performance to predict whether a student is falling off track, reviewed weekly or monthly.

children.name: Live Formative Checks
children.blurb: Live formative checks are quick, low stakes assessments during a lesson, such as mini whiteboard questions or short online polls, that show a teacher whether students understand before moving on.

children.name: Readiness Estimates
children.blurb: Readiness estimates are predictions, drawn from benchmark results, of which students are likely to pass state tests, and schools use them to direct support before the test.

children.name: Benchmark and Item Analysis
children.blurb: Benchmark and item analysis is the practice of using several-times-a-year benchmark assessments and question-level results to see how students are progressing toward standards and where instruction needs to change.

children.name: Growth, Mastery, and Proficiency
children.blurb: Growth data shows how much students have learned over time, while proficiency data shows where they stand against a standard, and both matter because a school with students far behind may show strong growth while proficiency stays low.

children.name: Reporting to Families
children.blurb: Reporting to Families means turning assessment data into plain-language progress reports that parents can understand and act on, delivered in time to help and in the family's own language.

children.name: Student Self Assessment
children.blurb: Student self assessment asks students to judge their own work against clear criteria and set their own goals for improvement, so they take charge of their learning rather than waiting for the teacher to direct it.

children.name: Portfolios, Performance Tasks, and Oral Assessment
children.blurb: Portfolios, performance tasks, and oral assessment are three ways to capture what students know and can do beyond what a standard test measures.

children.name: Assessing Learning When Students Have AI
children.blurb: AI has changed what some assessments can tell teachers, because a take home essay or problem set may now show what a tool can do rather than what a student can do.

children.name: Survey Analysis for School Improvement
children.blurb: Survey analysis for school improvement means using surveys of students, families, and staff to see experiences that test scores cannot show, then grouping open responses into themes with AI features in spreadsheet tools and checking that grouping by hand.

children.name: Building Data Skills in Staff
children.blurb: Building data skills in staff means giving teachers and leaders the training to read assessment data well, including its limits and uncertainties.

children.name: What Data Cannot Tell You
children.blurb: Data only captures part of a student's life and learning, so decisions about students should combine data with what adults know from knowing the student.

children.name: Fairness Checks
children.blurb: Fairness checks are routine reviews of a data system's results to see whether it treats groups of students differently, even when no one intended harm.

children.name: Program Evaluation
children.blurb: Program evaluation is the practice of checking whether a program or tool actually produced the gains it promised, by comparing students who used it with similar students who did not.

children.name: Board and Accountability Reports
children.blurb: AI can help school staff draft board reports, campus improvement plans and accountability documents by summarising data in plain language and organising large data sets.

children.name: Protecting Student Data
children.blurb: Protecting student data means limiting what schools collect, who can see it, and how long it is kept.

sections.body: This part of school life is the use of assessment results, data systems and early warning flags to notice which students need help and whether programs are working. The book describes AI here as a tool that can speed up benchmark and item analysis, growth and mastery reporting, fairness checks, program evaluation and reports for boards, while also warning that predictions can mislead. It points to research showing that a single accuracy number makes predictions look more reliable than they are, because running the same prediction with slightly different samples changes which individual students get flagged. It also notes that machine learning can improve early warning indicators and create clear rules, but that black box models invite staff to read results through their own assumptions. The chapter treats assessment data as something that starts conversations about students and never ends them.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: What works, according to the book, is data that leads to action: flags that produce outreach, fairness checks by group, program evaluations with comparison groups, and privacy rules that remove names and identification numbers before analysis in any tool not covered by a signed data privacy agreement. What does not work is the dashboard nobody acts on, where a district buys a platform, builds dashboards and holds meetings but no one follows up with the students the data identifies, or where hidden scores are interpreted through staff assumptions. The rule the chapter holds to is that data starts conversations and never ends them, and that data used to label rather than help causes harm. The board question is whether the district's data leads to help for students, and a dashboard alone does not answer it. The common failure is data becoming a ritual rather than a tool for helping students.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages fit together as a chain from noticing to acting to checking. A teacher or leader would start with The Early Warning System and Live Formative Checks to see who needs help now, then move to Readiness Estimates, Benchmark and Item Analysis, and Growth, Mastery, and Proficiency to understand what the data shows. Reporting to Families, Student Self Assessment, Portfolios, Performance Tasks, and Oral Assessment, and Assessing Learning When Students Have AI cover how results are shared and how students show what they know. Survey Analysis for School Improvement and Building Data Skills in Staff support the adults who read the data, while What Data Cannot Tell You and Fairness Checks set the limits and the equity test. Program Evaluation and Board and Accountability Reports turn the record into decisions about investments, and Protecting Student Data holds the privacy rule that runs through the whole chapter.
sections.heading: How these pages fit together
